notable_absence.finding: The single largest vocabulary gap this batch exposed: the registry has NO part-whole predicate. Nine rounds and 64 predicates produced not one composition relation, because a reference page decomposes a STATEMENT into clauses (modeled as cb:StatementOption/hasOption, a syntax relation) and never decomposes a RUNNING SYSTEM into processes. This page is almost entirely composition - 15 of its 30 relations are hasInternalComponent - so without that predicate the page yields almost nothing. Note also what the composition tree looks like: it is three levels deep (Data Service -> KV Engine -> Managed Cache -> Partition Hash Table), it mixes kinds of part freely (a network process, a per-bucket facility set, a memory structure, a thread class), and the page gives no vocabulary distinguishing those kinds. I used one flat predicate rather than invent a typed hierarchy the source does not support, but reconciliation should know the flattening is mine, not the document's. Two smaller gaps: no predicate for a default value (hasDefaultDuration, minted, 2 occurrences on this one page), and no predicate for conformance to an external standard (requiresEncodingStandard, RFC 8259). NOTHING WAS DROPPED for lack of evidence on this page.
notable_absence.second_finding: One thing on this page I could NOT extract as a relation and am reporting instead of forcing: the Managed Cache paragraph describes the write path as an ordered pipeline - 'When written, items enter the cache, and subsequently are placed onto a replication queue, so as to be replicated to one or more other nodes; and (in the case of items for Couchbase buckets) onto a disk queue, so as to be written to disk.' That is a sequence/dataflow fact (A then B then C), and the registry has no ordering predicate except requiresPriorExecutionOf, which is about a user running one statement before another, not about internal stages of a write. I omitted rather than abuse it. The Index Service page has the same problem worse (see index-service.json).

cross_component_finding: (1) TYPO: 'For more information on the Data Service' threading model' - a stray apostrophe where a possessive 's' belongs. I quoted it verbatim in the seeAlso evidence because the gate demands verbatim, so the ontology now contains a typo faithfully; worth a docs fix. (2) The Flusher's description, 'Deletes every item in the bucket', is stated with no warning at all next to an activation link, which is a strikingly bare presentation of a destructive operation on a conceptual page - contrast the Views deprecation on indexes.md, which does get an IMPORTANT admonition. (3) This page and services.md state the Data-Service-on-at-least-one-node rule in different words ('at least 1 node in the cluster' / 'at least one node of every cluster') and both link the same manage-data-service-and-rebalance.md target; the duplication is benign here but is the third place that same fact appears. (4) The page's component names (Dispatcher, KV Engine, Supervisor-equivalents, Scheduler) appear only in an image alt-text plus a bullet list; the architecture diagram itself is a PNG, so an agent consuming this corpus gets the component NAMES but not the ARROWS between them. Every dataflow fact on this page had to come from prose that happens to restate the diagram, and where the prose does not restate it, the relation is simply unrecoverable. That is a real limit on extracting architecture from these docs, and it applies identically to query-service.md and index-service.md.
cross_product_finding: No Capella or SDK page in the corpus decomposes the Data Service. The registry's sdk:kv-operations is the client-side mirror of everything on this page - get/insert/upsert/replace/remove - and the two never meet: the SDK tree documents the API, this page documents the machine, and nothing links a KV operation to the Dispatcher that handles it or the Managed Cache it lands in. I deliberately did not mint that link, since no page states it. Also worth noting for the ontology's naming discipline: 'KV' names three different things across the corpus - sdk:kv-operations (a client API family), privilege:capella-advanced-access-data-read (described in the registry as 'KV-level read access'), and data-service:kv-engine (a server-side component) - a fourth instance of the same-word-different-layer pattern already documented for 'role' and 'index'.
